Abkhaz has a complex system of three demonstratives. The first two clearly distinguish degrees of distance, while the third can either distinguish a further degree of distance or indicate invisibility (including the invisibility of a nearby object). Because the system can distinguish both three levels of distance and visibility, we encode it as having three distance levels as well as a visibility distinction.

The third demonstrative deictic in Abkhaz can be used to refer either to far away objects that are still visible or to invisible objects irrespective of distance (e.g. something behind a wall or behind the speaker and addressee's back). Because this deictic can mark both a third level of distance and invisibility, we encode the language both as having a visibility distinction, as well as distinguishing three levels of distance (see Dem-01).

The attributive function is mostly taken over by 1) nouns, 2) nominalized verbs, 3) AD-forms. Many property concepts are indeed expressed by syntactic nouns (e.g. 'big', 'bad', 'red', 'black', 'fierce', 'raw', etc), and this is why we coded Noun for Panaré. The AD-form category – adverb/adjective – is mostly derived via suffixes (possibly clitics), some of which attach to nominal roots, but also conjugated verb forms. Only 3 forms are not derived, and express non-numerical quantifier semantics (all, many/much (+epistemic value), some/many/lots), which we did not consider to be core property concept semantics.

Kambaata has a fully grammaticalised -ókkoo-paradigm to express the apprehensive meaning. No parallels are found in neighbouring languages or related languages. The primary function of this paradigm is to express warnings to the addressee. In the form of the first grammatical person, the paradigm is not only serving as a warning, but as a potential threat too. With the second grammatical person, the paradigm tends to express a prohibitive (p. i-iii). The apprehensive is exclusively used as a final verb in main clauses, can govern all types of subordinate clauses and belongs to the class of main verbs (p. vi). The typological classification does not seem to be an easy task. Judging from morphological aspects, the apprehensive patterns with affirmative indicative main verbs. Other criteria suggest that the apprehensive is better considered to be a type of directive verb together with the imperative and the jussive since it shares semantic features with the negative imperative as well as the jussive. The apprehensive cannot be relativized and may not be combined with the past and counterfactual particle “ikke” (p.vi). In Kambaata, the apprehensive distinguishes between seven bipartite, discontinuous subject indexes, of which the first element precedes and the second element follows the apprehensive morpheme -ókkoo: 1sg, 2sg, 3m, 3f/3pl, 3hon, 1pl, and 2pl/2hon (p. viii). The apprehensive seems also used with reported speech as some excerpts of the book "Le petit prince" show (p. x). The apprehensive does not seem restricted in terms of the verb forms that can be used (p. xi). When using the apprehensive, the worried speaker and the addressee can be the same person (p. xii). Kambaata does not impose a threat reading on [+control] verbs: The ‘hit’-verb can equally well be used for a warning (p. xiii). Semantic differences between the apprehensive and the negative imperative are hard to pinpoint, native speakers often accept to swap (p. xv), but apprehensive tends to express warnings of unintended, undesirable actions and the negative imperative prohibitions of actions that the addressee carries out wilfully (p. xvi). The apprehensive is only used in main clauses, and since Kambaata is a head-final language, the apprehensive only appears sentence finally (p. xvii). The apprehensive is assumed to have a language-internal, phrasal origin and to be the result of the merger of a complex verb form consisting of a same subject affirmative purposive converb and the existential copula “yoo-” (to be, exist) (p. xix -xxv).
Source: treisforthcapprehensive[ i-iii, vi, viii, x, xi, xii, xiii, xv, xvi, xvii,  xix -xxv]

Bright (1957: 139-140) reports on the vetative "xay" which carries two separate functions. First use: Normally precedes a predicate and expresses a warning as in xay imcax -> “Watch out you don't get burned!”. Second use: The second xay is postfixal, conditioning progressive accentuation. In this form it is also added to nouns (preceding all other postfixes) occurring only in the presence of pu=.....= ara, which strengthens the negative meaning. For example: "Not a single one lay there” (p.140). Not to be confused with the negative suffix -xay that the language uses to express a negation translated by "not". Nothing in garrett2020karok.

The plural act(ion) morphemes are highly irregular and apply to the entire lexicon. Motion verbs forgo the highly irregular plural act(ion) morphemes and instead have a much more regular plural motion morpheme.

The plural act(ion) and plural motion morphemes can refer to plural P or E repetition. Oswalt specifically delimits the cases where they can be used. For instance, a man picking up two marbles in a single act is marked with plural action (because P is plural), or if the man picks up one marble twice (because E recurs). Cases where plural A act on the same P (such as two men touching the same sofa) are interpreted by Oswalt as marking plural E (the acts of touching are independently acted events). On intransitives, it must mark event pluractionality.

It seems to carry an apprehensive in the first function, since it is mainly used to express the speaker's perspective and the examples are coded in direct speech. This might be a construction which is necessary to enable people to utter an apprehensive with the prefixed grammatical marker m(a)-, although it is hard to say from only four examples in sum.

The suffix -n which is used in an apprehensional context, is also used as an exhortative (but only in religious contexts). The suffix is formally not distinguishable from the use as a negative imperative, although "Sevo", a particle which means "holy" or "taboo" often accompanies the negative imperative use. Terill makes a distinction within the apprehensional use between an admonitive use and a deleterious possibility. While the admonitive use is used as a warning and sometimes implied as a negative imperative, the "deleterious possibility" is pointing out the possibility of something, but with no implication to avoid it. If nested with a HAB marker, the suffix -n does not seem to convey an admonitive function anymore (Terill 2003:96). The suffix -n which is used in an apprehensional context, is also used as an exhortative (but only in religious contexts). The suffix is optically not distinguishable from the use as a negative imperative, although "Sevo", a particle which means "holy" or "tabu" often accompanies the negative imperative use. Terill here distinguishes within the apprehensional use between an admonitive use and a deleterious possibility. While the admonitive use is used as a warning and sometimes implied as a negative imperative, the "deleterious possibility" is pointing out the possibility of something, but with no implication to avoid it. The S/A plurality morphemes are totally lexically specified. From a set of prefixes {uu-, n-, t/sh-, a-}, vocalic ablaut, and a set of suffixes {-sh, -v}, verbs select a combination to mark duality and plurality. Sometimes the same set which marks duality in one verb may mark plurality in another. Some of these (such as the suffixes) cannot occur alone, but must be together with one of the others. There appears to be no regularity to this system. We do not know if there are some verbs that lack this, as the grammar only states that "most" verbs have dual and plurals formed through the application of these processes, and counterexamples are not given.

The grammar describes pluralization with suffixes whose presence is conditioned based on preceding suffixes. Another analysis (the one we take) is that these suffixes actually have two variants, a singular variant and a plural variant, and some of the plural forms share similarities. The plural forms add a -rga- (Tarma dialect) or -rka- (San Pedro de Cajas dialect) before the durative marker -ya-, after any suffix that includes -ku-, and after the derivational suffix -na. The plural forms add a -ri- (both dialects) after the perfective marker -ru-, sequential marker -rgu-/-rku-, after any suffix that includes -ku-, and derivational suffixes. The distinction between adjective and verb categories in Nuuchahnulth is extremely slight, and the categorization of them as a separate category (e.g. Nakayama 2001) or a subcategory of verbs (e.g. Jacobsen 1979) differs by source. We code this as a proper adjective class, but note that the distinction is subtle. The distinctions that Inman knows about between the adjective and verb classes at the time of this coding are: (1) Adjectives (and nouns) have a reduced number of aspectual forms compared to verbs (limited largely to continuative and durative); (2) the incorporation of adjectives into a transitive suffixing verb is inevitably interpreted as modifying the (possibly elided but possibly overt) nominal object, while the incorporation of a verb stem into a verb (when this is possible) is interpreted as expressing the manner of the action; (3) some adjectives can take irregular plural marking, which is invariably one of the strategies of nominal plural marking, most of which are unavailable to verbs (Inman 2021).
It is difficult to distinguish sometimes between adjectives and verbs, but Inman believes the adjective class is probably open.

In Inman's experience (and that of linguists he contacted), the /t/ series sounds very alveolar. However, in Carlson et al 2001, the series is described as denti-alveolar. This determination was made based on one speaker, and upon follow-up it was determined that "denti-alveolar" did not mean that the sound had to be made on the teeth but just was slightly more forward, between the dental and alveolar places of articulation. There may be more variation in the /t/ series than is known, but in Inman's judgment it is, for most speakers and most of the time, produced at the alveolar ridge and without contact with the teeth.

There are two somewhat frozen plural verb morphemes: -!aqa, and -RL.yu (reduplication + long base + -yu). The Sapir-Thomas texts suggest that -!aqa was more productive in the past, but it is not clear how much more productive: It may have been fully a monoexponential plural, or not. Modern speakers do not generally recognize -!aqa suffixed on new verbs, so in the present day it is definitely frozen. -RL.yu seems to have been restricted by the time of the Sapir-Thomas texts as well. In our notes, -!aqa is used for: 'play', 'fight', 'bathe', and -RL.yu for 'speak', 'invite', and maybe 'say' (although here it has an unpredictable -ł, which may indicate different morpheme). In the Nootka Texts, more -!aqa verbs are present, including (but not limited to): 'work', 'swallow', 'go home', 'escape', 'troll/fish', 'make a boat'.
This is probably not an accurate number, and it is difficult to get one. -!aqa and -RL.yu forming plurals are lexicalized at this point, but a full list is hard to determine.

There is a dedicated small class of adverbs, which express manner, time and place. They are exclusively predicative, but can be nominalized to modify a noun – except for 2 adverbs, 'small' and 'big', which can modify the noun as they are, without derivation (silva2011rikbaktsa:204) ('big' is actually transparently derived from a noun). Property concepts are expressed via verbs ('be.beautiful', 'be.clean', be.good', etc.). Their use as noun modifiers is not described, probably because they are (only) used predicatively. It seems like an edge case because property concepts are expressed via verbs, but the fact that they seem to be only used predicatively makes them more similar to languages like Ese Ejja and Hixkaryana.

There is a complicated, unpredictable and extensive pattern of verbal subject plural marking, which encompasses the entire lexicon and is typically (if not always) intertwined with pluractionality, i.e. 4 forms for verbs: (1) sg-subj sg-event, (2) sg-subj pl-event, (3) pl-subj sg-event, (4) pl-subj pl-event. The forms that this plural marking can take are: (1) suffixation (many suffixes are used, for pl-subj sg-event this list includes -tim, -ta, -tax, -tox, -tx, -xam, -χ, -χam); (2) deletion of the post-tonic (i.e. stressed) vowel (which occurs for both sg and pl verbal forms, and it is unpredictable which form has the deletion); (3) substitution (sg /k/ -> pl /xk/, sg /i/ -> pl /ko/, sg /n/ or /t/ -> /ɬ/, and various ablauts); (4) infixation (mostly <ko>). There is a final set of verbs that fully supplete, but these are expanded upon in the SG-PL feature.

There are two forms to this monoexponential plural: an infixing or suffixing (depending on the verb) -a- and -aʔ-, with the former looking like it probably derives historically from the latter. The introduction of this morpheme can cause the preceding vowel to change from ə to e or a (likely a historical e,a -> ə change, probably only in monosyllabic words), and sometimes an ee to aya (probably also a historic contraction). The application of these forms is now completely unpredictable, and between the fieldwork of Boas and Kinkade it seems like this pattern began falling out of use.
The presence of the glottal stop in the infix -a(ʔ)- is unpredictable, as are vowel changes that it causes to the stem (although this is probably from an historical schwa-ization pattern).

Though the argument marked for plurality in transitive verbs is not explicitly mentioned in either the grammars of Boas or Kinkade, in his work on verbal suppletion in Salishan, Kinkade mentions that plural verbs always mark the object of a transitive as plural. This is likely true of the monoexponential plural as well, and the use of the singular 'it' in singular verb translations (e.g., 'teach it', 'see it') strongly suggests that it is the P argument that is marked for plurality.

When Boas gives examples of the infixing -a- he begins by showing examples of it on nouns (where it is again sometimes a suffix, instead of an infix). In the verbal section, some of the verbs look like they have attributive meanings, but it is unclear if these are real adjectives or simply attributive verbs. It is possible that the marker is also used on verbs, as well.
A list of forms is given in kinkade1981salish, and this is apart from the somewhat unpredictable but much more widespread -a(ʔ)- infix, which we treat as an irregular monoexponential plural.
However, there is an irregular infixing monoexponential plural -a(ʔ)- which is sometimes accompanied by vowel change.

Urarina shows number agreement on verbs and has several optional plural markers (mostly, plurality has to be inferred from the context). However, these plural markers are heavily intertwined with person marking, i.e. constrained on distinct person marking, and therefore cannot be considered as monoexponential plural markers. There is also suppletive sg-pl morphology that is limited to the intransitive verbs of posture, shape and color. However, it also encodes BIG vs SMALL entities, so it is not monoexponential plural per se.

There are 4 types of derivational morphology limited to mostly posture verbs (to basically derive A stative, B inchoative, C causative, D causative-stative) which have suppletive forms for number. Derivational morphology type A has 4 distinctions (sg, dual, paucal, greater plural, and distributive plural which we don't consider), type B has 3 (sg-paucal-pl) and types C and D have 2 (sg-non.sg). Some of these derivational morphemes are also available for shape and colour intransitive verbs. Altogether, there are about 100 verbs for which the derivational morphology is available. On top of the number distinction, there is a bipartite distinction (suppletive again) for BIG and SMALL.

The different sources on this language have conflicting data. Every verb takes either a suffix or prefix (or both) that inflects for the number of at least one of the verb's arguments. Which form the affix takes is highly dependent on verb class and even which lexical verb they attach to.
Prefix vs. suffix can be determined by word class (intransitive A, intransitive B, and transitive), however the precise form of the affix is highly lexically conditioned.

There are two slots in which a (highly morphophonologically irregular) monoexponential plural can appear: a prefix slot and a suffix slot. On transitives, the A role plurality is indexed by the suffix and the P role by the prefix. Intransitives fall into two classes (which might be either partially or wholly predictable based on their semantics, unergative vs. unaccusative), one of which takes a prefix and the other of which takes a suffix. So really this language has something like a Split-S system for plural marking.

There are 4 patterns (plus SG/PL stem alternation): 1) sg root + VVm: VERB-VVm; 2) sg root in -ech- (minus SG -ech-): VERB.ech- > VERB-VVm (mostly motion verbs); 3) sg root in -o'rep-: VERB-o'rep- > VERB-VVmah (verbs of running); 4) sg root in -ep-: VERB-ep- > VERB–ah (includes verbs of feeling) -- plus suppletion which is reported in the SG-PL stem alternation questionnaire.
